claude.via: Claude Code subagent (Agent tool), not the API

claude.reason: Rav Yehuda's ruling is said to arise from an incident that took place, but the incident is only alluded to, not narrated.
An incident is cited as precedent (bill lost, halitza required) but only alluded to in one line; one event followed by a ruling.
Terminological discussion and Rabbi Hiyya's teachings; nothing happens.
Legal discussion about the biblical David and Bathsheba incident, which is referenced, not narrated.
A statement and reports of sages' practice regarding orla; no incident leads anywhere.
Orphans come before Rava, he rules, the sages challenge and he justifies; one event followed by a ruling and legal discussion.
Rabbi Yehuda's report of a yevama coming to perform halitza before Rabbi Tarfon, who instructs them to call out; one event, mainly speech, cited as proof.
A narrated incident (man picking dates, woman asks, he proposes betrothal) followed by a ruling; mostly speech with little change.
Purely a scholarly question and answer between Rava bar Rav Hanan and Abaye.
Legal rulings and a baraita describing a hypothetical case; no event that happened.
The Queen Helene nazirite incident is only alluded to via Beit Hillel's ruling and must be filled in from context.
Eyewitness report of a woman coming before Ameimar, the brothers' remark and his silence; an incident cited as evidence, mainly speech with little change.
A man gives a conditional divorce and after thirty days claims he tried; real events but mostly speech and the outcome is left to legal discussion.
Two first-person anecdotes of food brought and shared with the attendant; real events but weak causality and change, cited as evidence.
Someone comes before Rav Yosef, who rules, followed by ordinary scholarly challenge; coming before the rabbi is the only event.
A couple comes before Rav Nahman, he recognises her accent, rules, is corrected and reverses; some event and change but mainly dialogue and ruling.
Exegetical derivation of Moses' birth and death dates; no narrated incident.
A woman seizes a silver cup toward her ketuba and demands sustenance; Rava rules. One real event followed by a ruling.
A scribe comes before Rabbi Abbahu and a legal Q&A follows; coming before the rabbi is the only narrated event.
A hypothetical legal question, a search for a source, and a ruling sent out; ordinary scholarly process with no incident.
A sage states a halakha and is rebuked; ordinary rabbinic dialogue, not conflict in the R-C2 sense.
Medical advice reported in Abaye's mother's name; general statements, no event.
Rabbi Hiyya teaches a ruling publicly twice and receives different reactions; teaching speech-acts with a small narrated reaction.
Rabbi Elazar recites a ruling before Shmuel and is mocked; later Rabbi Zeira, travelling to Israel, finds it taught there and retorts. Mainly speech with some events and conflict.
Rav Nahman visits Sura and answers halakhic questions; standard scholarly dialogue with no conflict or change.
A man comes before R. Hanina with a question and receives a sharp ruling; coming before the rabbi is the only narrated event (R-C0's limit, like Ketubot 50b:4).
Purely legal discussion of conflicting attributions and halakhic principles; no event is narrated.
A Sage reports a teaching to another, who replies with a different version of the tradition; ordinary scholarly transmission with no event or conflict.
Ravina finds R. Nahman bar Yitzhak pondering a dilemma that remains unresolved; a bare frame for a legal question with no action leading anywhere.
A baraita describing a custom and rulings about wedding days; a custom with no one-time event.

A slave immerses a gentile woman for intimacy and Rav Yosef rules on her status, followed by two brief incidents of men called 'son of an Aramean' and rulings; one real event each, then legal reasoning.
A dispute over attribution of a ruling, settled by Rav Mordekhai recalling what Rav Ashi said; scholarly transmission of speech without a real event or change.

Rabbis intend to act on a baraita, and an old woman tells them of her own incident in which Rav Nahman prohibited it; there is a real event and an implied change, but the incident is only alluded to and the rest is legal discussion.
Rabbi Abba teaches, Rav Safra objects, and Rabbi Abba reports the chain of questions to Rav; standard rabbinic dialogue with no event.
The Sages seek to permit the Gibeonites and Rabbi objects with an argument; considering a ruling is quasi-speech and the exchange is ordinary halakhic debate.
People cast aspersions on two men's lineage and rabbis rule they are valid; something happened to someone and a rabbi responded, but it is one event followed by a ruling.

The death of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: the Sages' fast and prayers, the maidservant's prayer and throwing the jug, his death, bar Kappara's announcement and Rabbi's final prayer; multiple actions with clear causality and change.
Rav Hisda's objection quoting a mishna about legal cases; no narrated event.
A habitual description of what Rav Hisda would say when such cases came before him, followed by exegetical discussion; a custom with no one-time event.
A man deposits a silver goblet with Hasa, Hasa dies without instructions, and Rav Nahman rules on ownership; an incident with more than one action followed by a ruling, like R-C0's cow case.
An incident is said to have come before R. Yitzhak but nothing of it is narrated; only his ruling is given.
Bar Haddaya consults two sets of rabbis who give differing rulings; coming before rabbis is the only event and the rest is halakhic speech.
Abaye invites questions and a Sage challenges his exegesis; ordinary scholarly back-and-forth with no event.

R. Tarfon's eyewitness account of ascending the platform and hearing the High Priest conceal the Name is a real event, but it has little causality or change and serves as evidence for a historical practice.
R. Elazar questions an elder about a past case where a court permitted a woman to remarry; the incident is only alluded to and must be reconstructed from context.
R. Zeira avoids his teacher because he wants to emigrate against his teacher's view; a real action with conflict, but only the opening of a narrative, followed by legal-exegetical justification.
Rava coerced Rav Natan bar Ami and collected 400 dinars for charity; a real event cited as precedent, with minimal narrative development.
Legal analysis of the style of a mishna; no event.
R. Ami and R. Asi consider a ruling and R. Yaakov bar Idi rebukes them; considering is quasi-speech and the rebuke is ordinary rabbinic discourse.
A man states his origin and R. Yitzhak Nappaha stands and declares where it is, followed by legal discussion; speech without conflict or change.

An actual incident is briefly recounted: a debtor improperly attached his money to a gentile and the Sages forced him to sell his land. It is one event plus a ruling, told only in summary inside a dialogue, so it is borderline.
Ravina's collection of the dowry is cited as a precedent. The ruling is the only act, and no other narrated action or change goes with it.
Ravin bar Hanina states a halakha and Rav Hisda sharply questions it. This is ordinary rabbinic dialogue, with no event and no real conflict.
Rav Ami's ruling, the Sages' challenge and his response are mostly speech. There is conflict and an implied change, so it is borderline (the shape of Ketubot 7a:1).
A baraita records that Rabbi ruled like Rabbi Ya'akov, cited only as a usage of the term 'ruled'. It is a bare report of a ruling and nothing happens.
These are general laws for a wedding interrupted by a death, with conditions and qualifications. Nothing in them happened to anyone.
A scribe confesses that he wrote the divine names without proper intent, and Rabbi Ami rules that he loses his wage. There is a prior act and a consequence, but it is mainly a dialogue and a ruling.
People come before Rabbi Ami and he gives a ruling. Coming before a rabbi is the only event, and no other action or change is narrated.
An exchange of letters about a halakhic question, which is quasi-speech. The mild challenge is ordinary scholarly back-and-forth, not conflict, and no event follows.
Rav Yehuda's general ruling about kidnapped women, and the Rabbis' objections, are a legal discussion of a class of cases, not a narrated incident.
Rabba reports finding the Sages discussing a dispute and giving them his view. It is purely scholarly discussion, with no event.

Embedded in the letter is Ilfa's incident: a man pining for a woman sought to leave the Land, heard the teaching, and stayed and suffered until he died. It has several actions, causality and change. The letter's advice in [3]-[4] is not narrative.
Rav Huna's ruling on converting a minor, and the Gemara's analysis of it, are pure legal discussion.
Orphan daughters come before Shmuel, who rules on their support. Coming before the rabbi is the only event, which is not a story (Ketubot 50b:4).
The passage is only the opening words of an incident (a man's instruction in his will) that is completed in the following segment. At most it is part of a case of one event followed by a ruling.
This is a general custom of David's soldiers and an exegesis of a verse, offered as a legal explanation. No narrated event is in the passage itself.
Hypothetical legal dilemmas about illness and menstruation delaying a wedding. No event happened.
Rava explains a hypothetical case of a general coming to a city. This is legal analysis, not a narrated event.
This is a hypothetical scenario of witnesses raising and lowering a man's priestly status, built to explain a dispute. It is a legal case, not an event.
A man's will leaves a dowry, prices then fall, and Rav Idi rules on the surplus. It is a real case, but one event plus a ruling with little change, so it is borderline rather than not.
These are legal inferences about a groom's obligation to provide sustenance, framed as general cases. Nothing happened.

An institutional history: the court raised widows' marriage contracts when priests demeaned widows, then restored them when men avoided widows. There are events, causality and change, but they are collective and habitual, told as legal background.

A man testifies before Reish Lakish and Rabbi Elazar challenges him. This is the first half of an incident that is completed only in the following context (Reish Lakish's harsh look). On its own it is mostly speech and part of a story.
A woman comes before Ameimar, her brothers speak, and he stays silent. This is cited as evidence of his view. Coming before the rabbi is the only event, and the rest is speech.
A description of Mar Zutra's practice in writing a halitza document, an objection, and a ruling. The narrative does not continue (Yevamot 106b).
A student questions his father's ruling and is told to be silent; this is speech only, and a rebuke like this is ordinary rabbinic dialogue rather than conflict that makes a story.
The Talmud cites the Mishnah's incident of the five women only by allusion and then derives halakhot from it; one incident plus a ruling, followed by legal analysis.
A legal statement and an objection from a hypothetical mishnaic case; nothing is narrated as having happened.
A Mishnah reporting a teaching expounded before the Sages at Yavne; no event beyond the teaching and no conflict.
Rabbi falls ill and is moved to Tzippori: real events, but only a fragment of his death narrative, embedded in Gemara harmonization with little change.
Students ask Rabbi Eliezer a halakhic question and he answers; speech only, with no conflict or event.
A Mishnah stating a hypothetical case of competing claims and the Sages' opinions; it is a legal case, not an event that happened.
Ravina holds an orphan's wine, asks Rav Ashi and is told to take it along; some events and a ruling, but the change in outcome is at most implied.
Rabbi falls ill, Rabbi Hiyya visits and finds him crying, and they exchange words; real events and emotion, but it is mainly dialogue with little change.
The Sages award Nakdimon's daughter a large perfume allowance, and she blesses them and they answer amen; one real event followed by speech, with little further change.
The Sages challenge Ben Azzai for not practicing what he preaches and he answers; speech only, but with personal conflict over his life choice.
A goat drank blacksmith's water and was found to have no spleen when slaughtered; events with causality, but it is cited only as evidence for a remedy.
The Sidon tanner's widow incident is one event followed by the Sages' ruling, with an implied change; this is the Mishnah's own copy (R-C1).
Ravina holds an orphan's wine, asks Rav Ashi and is told to take it along; some events and a ruling, but the change in outcome is at most implied.
Descriptions of former wedding customs in Judea and the Galilee, with no one-time event.
A document is brought to Rava and Rav Pappa's testimony is rejected; after that it is all dialogue, with implied conflict over trust.
Rava retracts on the basis of a baraita describing a hypothetical slander case; legal discussion, not a narrated event.
A man whose brother died abroad asks Rabbi Hanina whether to go down for levirate marriage and is rebuked; one background event, then a question and a ruling.
Rav Hisda tells Rabba to study a baraita and Rabba does; a study frame for a halakhic explanation, with no conflict or change.
A hypothetical legal case about witnesses and a deed of gift, with two schools' opinions and the halakha.
Yudan's sons are freed and Rav Aha permits them to marry each other's wives, and Rava challenges him; one event followed by a ruling and ordinary debate.
A man testifies before Rabbi Ami and the man he testified about is elevated to the priesthood; essentially one incident plus a ruling, though the ruling produces a change of status.
Rabba reports finding scholars discussing a dispute and offering his view; standard scholarly dialogue with no event or conflict.
A halakhic clarification about where a groom and his menstruating wife sleep; no narrated event.
An exegetical inference about biblical Israel offering the omer before eating; a fragment of reasoning, not a narrated story.
A report of Rav Ashi's blessing practice on a visit, cited as halakhic precedent; nothing follows and no change occurs.
A one-line precedent (Rabbi gave one-twelfth) cited as evidence, a single act with no narrated change, followed by legal analysis.
Rava's habitual response to such cases is a speech-act practice with no particular event or change.
Legal discussion of a baraita about a hypothetical vow; no event narrated.
Halakhic transmission dispute and a sarcastic retort; ordinary rabbinic dialogue with a retraction (quasi-speech), no event.
A description of rabbis' seating arrangement followed by a discussion, exactly the Yevamot 17a case Jeff ruled not a story.
One real event (he held his wife's hand throughout the gentile occupation of Jerusalem) followed by the Sages' ruling; mainly testimony and ruling.
Pishon's wife's refusal is the Yevamot 107b case Jeff ruled not a story: one act mentioned without change or causality.
Mainly a halakhic query and answer, but a real event intervenes (Rav Huna dies before the question arrives, and his son answers).
A document brought before R. Abbahu and a colleague's correction; coming before a rabbi and a ruling is the only event.
Mostly dialogue between brothers, but with real conflict over the yevama and inheritance and an implied resolution (dividing the property).
R. Zeira's avoiding his teacher because he wished to emigrate is a real action with conflict, but little is narrated and it shifts to halakhic justification.
Habitual practices of R. Yohanan and Rava regarding elders, cited as practice; nothing follows.
Rav Nahman visits and is asked a halakhic question which he answers; speech with no conflict or change.
A hypothetical legal case and its derivation; no event happened.
Orphans come before Rava, he orders support and defends it against the Sages; essentially one event followed by legal discussion (cf. Jeff on Ketubot 51a).
The Gemara's commentary on R. Ya'akov's story of the boy who fell, not the story itself (the Kiddushin 39b case).
A man comes before Rabban Gamliel with a claim and receives a parable; mainly speech acts with an underlying event (Jeff's Ketubot 10a borderline).
Cases came before Rabbi and R. Yishmael and were ruled on, then a scholarly exchange; coming before a rabbi is the only event.
A man comes before Rabban Gamliel with a claim and receives a parable; mainly speech acts with an underlying event (Jeff's Ketubot 10a borderline).
Mishnah and halakhic discussion of betrothal periods and teruma; the only narrative element is a biblical verse analyzed exegetically.
Report of Rav's practice of sustaining orphan girls, followed by a conceptual dilemma; no event follows.
An actual incident is alluded to (conditional betrothal, then forced divorce) but only summarized as precedent for the ruling.
Mishnah incident: a girl is raped at the spring, followed by a ruling on her marriage; events with weak causality (Jeff's Ketubot 14b borderline).
Rav Yehuda's habitual difficulty and Ulla's advice citing others' practice; custom and speech with no conflict or change.
A halakhic dilemma raised by Reish Lakish and left unresolved; nothing happened.
The Tzaidan incident is only alluded to ("an incident in Tzaidan etc.") as the Gemara asks why the Mishnah cites it; the events are not narrated here.
A bill of divorce with an unusual dating is sent to Rabba as a question and he rules; the only narrated event is bringing the case for a ruling (R-C0's limit).
Two single acts (Rav Kahana taking a cloth, Mar bar Rav Ashi buying one) cited as precedents for a legal point, with no change or continuation.
A hypothetical case constructed by the Gemara ("with what are we dealing here"), not an event that happened.
A report of what Rav Kahana did with an orphan's beer, with his rationale, cited as practice; one act, no change or consequence.
A legal statement reported before Shmuel and his disagreement; ordinary scholarly exchange with no event.
Analytical explanation of why Abaye and Rava chose different sources; no event.
A man states his origin and R. Yitzhak Nappaha stands and responds, followed by legal-geographic discussion; mainly speech with a minimal event.
Rav Ashi's visit is the frame for reporting his practice of reciting wedding blessings; a description of practice with no change.
A rumor about a betrothal is sent to Abaye and he rules; the case coming for a ruling is the only event, with no further action or change.
Rava coerced Rav Natan bar Ami and extracted 400 zuz for charity: a real event with some change, but cited briefly as a precedent with no continuation.
Homiletic and anatomical teachings about ears and fingers; no event.

The Gemara quotes the Mishnah's incident (bill of divorce brought to Rabban Gamliel, which he validated), which R-C1 says may be included, but it is one event followed by a ruling and textual discussion.
A man deposits pearls with R. Meyasha, who dies without instructions; the parties come before R. Ami, who rules. An incident with several narrated events resolved by a ruling.
Rav Hisda's self-report about marrying at sixteen, a statement about himself with no narrated event or consequence.
Legal enactments and teaching advice, including Abaye quoting his mother; dicta, no event.
Tannaitic dispute and analysis about teruma allotments; no event.
Rabbi Natan asked Sumakhos a legal question and was answered; scholarly speech with no conflict or event.
Rav Safra's and Rava's habitual Shabbat preparations cited as practice; customs that lead nowhere.
Rav Kahana took a cloth at a redemption and declared its value: a single act cited as precedent, with no change or continuation.
Two brief first-person incidents (waiters given food and so spared danger), cited as evidence for a rule; real events but slight, with little change.
A habitual practice (daily meat for a poor man) followed by discussion of its novelty; a custom with no one-time event or change following.
A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya examined it to rule; one event followed by a ruling and legal discussion.
Analytical question about the practical difference between two opinions; no event.
One real event (men sinning with the maidservant in Pumbedita) followed only by Abaye's hypothetical statement and Ravina's ruling; no further action or change.
Abaye's retort to Ravin is ordinary scholarly back-and-forth with no event beyond speech.
A rumor circulated about a woman (one event), followed by a cited precedent and ruling; little action or change.
The Sages apportion wine to Nakdimon's daughter-in-law, she blesses them, and they pointedly withhold amen: several actions with a response and an ironic turn.
Pure legal analysis of konamot and liens; nothing happens.
A man comes before Rav Nahman and is ordered flogged: mainly speech with a ruling; segment 3 is the Gemara's commentary.
A bare report that R. Yohanan issued a ruling in Tzaidan, followed by discussion; no narrated event beyond the ruling.
Courts rule and collect from movables, and Rav Nahman threatens to reverse them: events and conflict, but mostly rulings with weak causality and implied change.
Men taunted as sons of Arameans, and rabbis rule on their status: one event followed by a ruling; segments 2-3 are legal explanation.
Halakhic objection and response between Amoraim; no event.
Rabbi Simlai's remark to his mamzer host is speech only, cited as evidence, with nothing following and no conflict.
Rav Malkiyyu married off the deaf-mute and wrote a ketubah, and Rava praises it: real actions but cited as a precedent, with little narrative development.
Rabbi Elazar sees a field and makes an aphorism to it; no event beyond seeing and speaking, no change.

The passage holds the end of the story begun in context (the man gave his property away, R. Yonatan forced his sons to feed him, the man kissed his feet); the rest of the segment is Gemara commentary.
A one-line report that Rabbi gave an orphan one-twelfth, cited as evidence; no narrative.
Rav Hanan visits Rav Kahana, sees an animal before him, and questions him: a real event but mainly dialogue; the Abaye/Rav Sheshet lines are bare practices.
Legal analogies and objections only; no event.
A son corrects his father's teaching and Shmuel rebukes him for disrespect: all speech, about teaching, with some interpersonal conflict.
Rabba bar bar Hana brings a partly-witnessed get and comes before R. Elazar, who rules: one event then a ruling, with no further change.
A legal statement and its analysis; no event.
A chain of theoretical halakhic dilemmas; nothing happens.
Scholarly objection and rebuttal about a ruling; ordinary Talmudic dialogue, not conflict in the R-C2 sense.
Levi expounds a law twice and is first not praised, then praised: an event with a reaction, but the actions are mainly verbal.
A legal discussion of an incident in the wagons of Tzippori with too little of the incident given.
The Gemara's explanation of what R. Akiva was thinking about the etrog; commentary, not story.
A woman obligated to swear comes to court; after that it is litigants' and judges' dialogue with a ruling and a rebuke, mainly speech with one real event.
Pure legal dialectic about minors' conversion; nothing happened.
A hypothetical challenge and answer between scholars; ordinary dialogue with no event.
Part of the condolence visit for Rav Hiyya bar Abba's son: Reish Lakish has his disseminator recite blessings, mainly speech; segment 4 is the Gemara's comment, not story.
Rav sends a question and Rabbi answers after Rabbi Hiyya's clarifying question; quasi-speech without real conflict or change.
A bare report of how Ravina allotted property, cited as evidence for a legal point; no response or consequence.
A legal objection from a mishna; no event.
An incident only alluded to, with Rafram pressuring Rav Ashi into a ruling and collection; one event followed by a ruling.
A difficulty unresolved for 22 years until Rav Yosef became head and resolved it; mostly teaching, with an event and some change.
Rav Huna and Rav Nahman visit the ill Rabba bar Avuh and ask him a question; mainly dialogue with minor events. Segment 4 is Gemara commentary.
A marriage contract is lost and the couple come before Rav Yosef, who rules; one real event followed by a ruling.
A man sets a conditional divorce, and when the date arrives he claims he said a different date; mostly speech followed by legal analysis.
Legal exposition of the mishna; no event.
Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef finds Rabbi Abbahu and learns the Usha teaching forty times; mainly teaching, which Jeff ruled borderline.
A man betroths a minor with vegetables in the market, then Ravina rules; one event followed by a ruling.
A mishna listing legal obligations; general law, not an event.
A dialogue between Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Elazar with conflict, an emotional reaction and a conciliatory turn; mainly speech.
A fragment of the account of Rabbi's illness: he falls ill and is moved to Tzippori, embedded in Gemara discussion; part of a story.
Rabbi Yosei travels to Netzivin, meets an elder and questions him; one real event, then mainly dialogue.
A question asked and answered, reported for its ruling; speech without conflict.
A legal dilemma; no event.
A report of what Rav Kahana did with an orphan's beer and his rationale; no response or consequence follows.
Rav Hamnuna teaches, the audience clamors against him, and Rav Yosef defends him; mainly speech with conflict.
A bare report of a blessing Rav Haviva recited, followed by a ruling against it; no development.
Exegetical discussion of verses; Shmuel's instruction to bring ten men is a cited speech, not a story.
Rav Nahman's visit to Sura only frames a halakhic question-and-answer; ordinary scholarly dialogue with no conflict or change.
A man deposited silk, the custodian died without instruction, they came before Rabbi Abba who ruled; narrated incident with actions and a change, resolved by a ruling (the cow shape).
Mostly legal discussion; the only narrative is a one-line allusion to an incident where a woman strangled her child, cited as evidence and not narrated.
A general dictum about bringing a child to school and its harmonization; no event.
A legal objection and answer from a mishna; no narrated event.
Legal discussion of wedding benedictions; the reference to Boaz is a proof-text, not a narrated story.
A baraita on Judean yield plus a Sadducee's remark praising his land; speech without conflict or a narrated event.
Rav's objection silences Shmuel's father and Rav then applies a mocking verse to him; mainly speech, but with conflict and a reaction (silence).
Abaye's boast and a scholar's challenge followed by a baraita; standard rabbinic dialogue without an event.
A man comes before R. Yehoshua ben Levi testifying to another's Levite status and he elevates him; one event and a ruling with a change of status, but little more narrated.
Rav Huna found the Sages sitting and discussing, and he answered them; a setting followed only by legal discussion (like Yevamot 17a).
Legal discussion of slave defects; no event.

Rabba bar Rav Huna taught publicly, was challenged, then appointed an interpreter and publicly retracted; mainly teaching/speech but with an action and a change (Jeff: low confidence at most on Gittin 43a).
R. Zeira finding R. Asi sitting and teaching serves only to transmit a ruling; no story.
R. Elazar only thought to rule and a student cautioned him; speech about a ruling not made, with no event or real conflict.
Rav Kahana brought a bill of divorce and asked Rav, who ruled; one routine act followed by a ruling and legal explanation.
A man's claim (speech) brought before R. Ami, a ruling and R. Asi's objection; coming before the rabbi is the only event beyond speech (R-C0 limit, Ketubot 50b:4).
Legal analysis of a mishna; no event.
An eyewitness report that a woman came before Ameimar and he stayed silent, cited as evidence of his view; coming before him is the only event and nothing follows.
Gemara's explanation of a government decree as background to a law; no narrated incident.
A difficulty unresolved for twenty-two years until Rav Yosef became head of the academy and resolved it; mainly teaching, but one real event with a change.
Rav Yehuda teaching his son quips that his mother is 'more bitter than death'; teaching speech with implied domestic conflict; segment 3 is Gemara commentary (R-B4).
Legal discussion of wedding celebration days; no event.
Rav Yosef mixed seeds and planted, Abaye challenged him, and he later retracted citing Rav's garden; one real action, then mainly dialogue with a change of view.
Legal discussion of Shmuel's rulings on vows; no event.
A man whose betrothed died comes before the rabbis and receives a ruling, followed by scholarly challenge; coming before them is the only event (R-C0's limit, as Ketubot 50b:4).
A Mishnah stating a hypothetical legal case and a dispute; nothing happened.
An incident is said to have come before R. Yitzhak, but nothing of it is narrated beyond his ruling; coming before the rabbi is the only event.
Two bare reports of how many wedding blessings Levi and Rav Asi recited, cited as evidence of practice; nothing follows.
Ordinary scholarly exchange about a custom, with an incident cited only as evidence of the practice; no consequence follows.
R. Yehuda reports an incident he was involved in only as the occasion of a ruling; no narrated action beyond the ruling.
Mostly an account of an ordinance, but it narrates that the Sages added cups, people became drunk, and the Sages restored the earlier rule: events with change, though collective and schematic.
Two transmitted versions of cases that came before Rabbi and R. Yishmael, known only by their rulings, followed by standard scholarly discussion.
Transmission of a teaching and a disagreement over its version; ordinary scholarly dialogue with no event.
Ameimar's permission and Rav Ashi's challenge are a ruling plus ordinary scholarly back-and-forth; no further action or change.
Bare reports of how many blessings were recited at two weddings, cited as evidence; nothing follows.
A bare report of Rav Zevid's ruling or practice, with no response or consequence.
Legal discussion of hypothetical cases; no event.
Ravina is taking his own wine to sell and asks Rav Ashi about the orphan's wine; a real situation and action precede the ruling, but the outcome is only implied.
Standard halakhic dialogue between Rav Pappi and Rav Pappa; no event.
Two cases where a father's will met a change in prices, followed by a ruling: real events and a change, but mainly one event then a ruling.

Mar Zutra compelled a rebellious wife to stay, and from that couple R. Hanina of Sura was born: an incident with action and consequence; the Gemara's rejection of it as precedent is commentary (R-B4).
A man whose betrothed died comes before the rabbis and is ruled on, then a scholarly challenge; coming before them is the only event (R-C0's limit).
The sages reclining in Lod debate study versus action and reach a consensus; mainly speech, with disagreement and a resolution but no event beyond speaking.
Levi intends to act on a baraita and Rav corrects him with a teaching; ordinary halakhic exchange with no event that follows.
A bare report that Rabba ruled on a found bill of divorce according to his view, with alternate versions of the place; no response or consequence.
Shapur's daughter: her mother ate etrogim and she was so fragrant she was placed before her father atop the spices; a brief anecdote with some causality, embedded in a list of folk sayings.
A baraita describing a hypothetical case and its law; no event that happened.
A man comes before R. Hanina to ask about levirate marriage and receives a sharp answer; coming before the rabbi and the reply are the only events.
R. Yehoshua answers a halakhic question and testifies about families' lineage as evidence; speech without conflict and a report cited as proof.
Mainly speech (the Rabbis urge him to marry, he deflects), but a real event lies behind it: he became impotent from Rav Huna's discourse.
A couple coming before Rav Yosef with competing claims; coming before the rabbi is the only narrated event, and the passage is a fragment.
Shmuel's instruction to Rav Hana is cited as a teaching about publicizing a halakha; speech only, no event or conflict.
Only a note on where the Mishnah's incident took place, inside legal discussion; nothing is narrated.
Hypothetical legal cases and their analysis; no event that happened.
A rabbi states a ruling and is sharply rebuked; ordinary scholarly back-and-forth with no other event.
Rabbis arrive in a town, are asked a question, debate, and go before the local rabbi who corrects them; mostly speech, with some events.
Rabba and Abaye's practice of Torah and kindness leads to longer lives than their cursed lineage allowed; there is a change, but it is reported briefly within exegesis, with weak narration.
A couple comes before Rav Nahman, who notices her accent and rules, then reverses his ruling when corrected; mostly dialogue, with a small change.
Mainly speech (the Rabbis urge Rav Sheshet to marry, he deflects), with a real underlying event: his impotence from Rav Huna's discourse.
One real event (betrothal with vegetables in the market) followed by a ruling; no further action or change.
A halakhic question-and-answer between Rav Hisda and Rav Yosef; standard dialogue, no event.
Two deeds come before Rav Yosef, he rules, and the losing party argues; coming before the rabbi and his ruling are the only events.
An incident cited briefly as evidence: the daughters raced ahead of the sons; real events, but only alluded to with little narration.
A question sent to a rabbi, which is a quasi-speech act with no further event within the passage.
A bare report that a wealthy man sent Rabbi gifts, followed by an explanation of the fabrics; one act with no change.
The Gemara quotes the Mishnah's Tzaidan incident only by allusion ('an incident in Tzaidan etc.') and then discusses it; an incident alluded to rather than narrated.
A bare report of a rabbi's ruling or his own practice; one act with no continuation or change.
A baraita stating a hypothetical legal case; nothing happened.
Legal discussion of a deathbed gift; no narrated event.
Exegetical teaching and a scholarly challenge to it; ordinary discourse, not a story.
A man comes before Rav Nahman with a claim, and Rav Nahman orders him flogged; mainly speech, with a minimal event and consequence.
Rav Pappa's instruction to Pappa the ox herder is cited as a precedent for a ruling; one act with no change.
One real event (a betrothal with silk) followed by a dispute over the ruling; segment 3 is legal discussion only.
Legal discussion that only alludes to the biblical David and Bathsheba incident; no story is narrated.
Elijah's advice to Rabbi Natan is a single piece of speech with no event, conflict or change.
Mar Yehuda finds the two scholars, poses a contradiction, they fall silent and go to Rabba, who rebukes the questioner; some events, but it is mainly a scholarly exchange.
Purely legal argumentation (Rav Nahman's objection and Rava's resolution); no narrated event.
Rabbi Yohanan's relatives come to him, he advises them to fix a sum with the doctor, and he later regrets acting like a legal advisor: events followed by a change of mind.
Rav Nahman arriving in Sura and being asked a halakhic question is only a frame for a legal answer; nothing else happens.
Rav Kahana holds an orphan's beer until the Festival and explains why: one real act with its rationale, little change or outcome.
Ravnai reports Shmuel's ruling, Ameimar praises it and Rav Ashi rebukes him: ordinary scholarly back-and-forth, which Jeff ruled not a story (Ketubot 21b:0).
Segments 2-4 are legal discussion; segment 5 only alludes to the incident of the woman who removed her husband from the grave, which must be filled in from commentaries.
Rav Aha's habit of dancing with the bride on his shoulders is a real action, followed by a question and his answer; mainly speech with no further change.
Hypothetical legal analogies and objections; no event is narrated.
A man comes before Rav Nahman with a claim and is ordered flogged; Jeff called Ketubot 10a borderline as it is mainly speech acts.

Continuation of Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav's case: after the ruling he houses his wife in his courtyard and arranges her comings and goings, real actions in response but habitual and with little further change.
